title: Four readers. Four independent paths.
intent: Keep the approved UI. Organize the content around the question each reader brings.

navigation.entry: All four audience regions are visible on one sheet.
navigation.order: Read the numbered content within a region. Pan and zoom to inspect it; no page turns or hidden sections.
navigation.ending: Each region has its own conclusion. Moving the view never opens another page.
navigation.address: The sheet URL preserves its center (x, y) and zoom (z).

shared.appearance: Keep the approved infographic, characters, illustrations and colors. Unfold existing UI references and source excerpts onto one sheet.
shared.evidence: Cite original passages beside the relevant claim. Distinguish recorded outcomes, live actions and proposed capabilities; quotation coverage is not implementation coverage.
shared.reuse: Reuse a diagram or recording when it answers the reader's question. Select the relevant moments; do not send the reader through the full regression laboratory.
shared.scope: All twelve proposed page summaries are visible. Existing screenshots are reference material; they do not imply that the proposed pages are already implemented.

branches.title: User
branches.question: What does this let me do?
branches.perspective: Alice wants to make a property proposal with her bank's approval.

pages.title: Start with Alice's goal
pages.show: The existing bank-to-property infographic: Alice, Northbank, Ben and Sofia, each with a clear role.
pages.message: A bank decision can enable a property proposal without sharing the bank's private papers.

pages.title: Follow the proposal
pages.show: Northbank approves → Alice proposes → Ben relays → Sofia receives. Each stop shows its consequence below the stable infographic.
pages.message: See who acts now, what changed and what happens next.

pages.title: Understand the ending
pages.show: The same purchase has two explicit endings in its carousel: proposal received, or financing declined and the proposal blocked.
pages.message: An approval enables the next action; a refusal cannot be treated as an approval.

branches.finish: I understand the journey and can recognize its outcome.

branches.title: Investor
branches.question: Why does this work, and what is proven?
branches.perspective: A technical evaluator wants the mechanism behind the product promise.

pages.title: Understand Daml and Canton
pages.show: Northbank's authorized Daml choice, separate participant views, and the scoped result that permits Alice to continue.
pages.message: Daml choices enforce who may act; the multi-participant example shows private details staying separate from shared progress.

pages.title: Connect independent applications
pages.show: Two supported paths into the same workflow core: implement its interface, or compile an adapter for an eligible existing DAR.
pages.message: The repository demonstrates reusable integration for bounded examples. The source application keeps its authority.

pages.title: Separate proof from ambition
pages.show: Local workflow evidence beside the remaining product questions: broader integration, independent adoption and release readiness.
pages.message: Working local examples are evidence; external adoption and unresolved guarantees still need their own proof.

branches.finish: I can explain the mechanism, the demonstrated scope and the remaining risks.

branches.title: Architecture
branches.question: How is the system designed?
branches.perspective: A reviewer wants to test whether the design satisfies the original intent.

pages.title: Locate each responsibility
pages.show: A diagram of browser, off-ledger Scala service, bindings, on-ledger Daml core and application contracts; show ownership and participant boundaries.
pages.message: Separate orchestration from authorization, and shared progress from private application state.

pages.title: Trace one command
pages.show: Request → typed service → ledger choice → observed state. A refused action stays visibly refused along that same route.
pages.message: A submitted request is not a committed result; the UI follows the state that was actually observed.

pages.title: Challenge the guarantees
pages.show: Three focused diagram stops: a refused authority bypass, an eligible atomic settlement, and progress recovered after reconnection. Pair each with its original claim and evidence.
pages.message: State exactly what each example proves. A staged workflow is not one atomic transaction, and a quoted requirement is not a passing test.

branches.finish: I can identify boundaries, trace execution and challenge a claim with evidence.

branches.title: Implementation
branches.question: Where do I read and verify the code?
branches.perspective: A senior developer wants one understandable route through a real feature.

pages.title: Find the feature
pages.show: The existing file tree and colored source view, with a concise explanation of the financing slice and its place in the repository.
pages.message: Product runtime, ledger contracts and book tooling have distinct homes; begin with one feature rather than the entire repository.

pages.title: Read the typed path
pages.show: The financing screen, shared API, Scala service, Daml choice and observation code, with purpose annotations beside the real source.
pages.message: Follow the actual types and functions that carry one action from the browser to an observed result.

pages.title: Verify the golden story
pages.show: Input → execution → actual result beside the committed expectation; connect the result to the same recorded infographic.
pages.message: A golden expectation is the regression baseline. A mismatch fails; an illustration alone does not establish correctness.

branches.finish: I know where to read, what owns each behavior and how it is verified.
